events.headline: Fuel, fertiliser costs strain American farmers' support for Republicans in midterms

items.title: Fuel, fertiliser costs strain American farmers' support for Republicans in midterms
items.summary: Farmers in the Midwest United States face surging diesel and fertiliser costs which are outpacing their incomes. The sector has seen diesel prices climb by 67 percent while fertiliser prices, at times, have seen steep price jumps. This comes amid trade along the Strait of Hormuz being disrupted by the US' conflict with Iran. Trade wars with China and Canada has also worsened the US agricultural market, raising doubts over their continued support for the Republican Party.

analysis.tldr: Troubles for farmers in America due to high fuel and fertiliser costs—driven by Middle East conflicts and trade wars—can ripple outward to global commodity prices and inflation, impacting everyday household costs in India.
the_story: Farmers in the Midwest United States are struggling with diesel costs jumping by 67 percent and steep rises in fertiliser prices.
These surging costs are outpacing the incomes of American farmers, putting a strain on their political support for the Republican Party in midterms.
The problems are caused by trade disruptions along the Strait of Hormuz due to the US conflict with Iran, alongside trade wars with China and Canada.
analysis.what_happened: Farmers in the US Midwest are facing a severe financial squeeze because the cost of diesel has spiked by 67 percent and fertiliser prices have jumped sharply. This happened because trade along the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted by the US conflict with Iran, and trade wars with China and Canada further damaged the US agricultural market.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local bakery where the price of flour and electricity suddenly doubles, but people aren't willing to pay more for bread, leaving the baker struggling to pay their bills.
why_it_matters_india: US conflicts and trade disruptions drive up global crude oil and energy costs.
Higher global energy costs make imported fuel and agricultural inputs pricier for India.
Costlier imports feed into domestic inflation (rising prices of everyday goods), which hurts common people.
If global economic stability wobbles due to US political and trade stress, foreign investors may pull money out, affecting Indian markets.

impacts.rationale: Disruptions near key shipping routes like the Strait of Hormuz restrict oil flow, pushing prices up—which is bad because it makes petrol and diesel more expensive in India.
Higher global fuel and fertiliser costs raise the price of transporting and growing food, translating to pricier goods for regular consumers.
When global energy prices rise, India has to spend more dollars to buy oil, causing the rupee to weaken (each rupee buys fewer dollars), making imports costlier.

watch_next: Developments in the Strait of Hormuz and Middle East conflict status
Updates on US trade relations with China and Canada
Global crude oil price movements
analysis.caveats: The article is quite short and focuses heavily on American domestic politics, so the exact scale of global spillover will depend on how long the shipping disruptions last.

events.headline: Telangana advises farmers to opt for crops requiring less water in rabi

items.title: Telangana advises farmers to opt for crops requiring less water in rabi
items.summary: Water shortage likely due to the continued impact of El Nino, says State Agriculture Minister Tummala Nageswara Rao

events.article_text:
The Telangana government has asked farmers to choose short-duration pulses and oilseeds that require less water and investment during the upcoming rabi (yasangi) season, citing likely water shortages due to the continued impact of El Niño.

“Farmers should choose crops based on the availability of irrigation water and market demand,” Telangana Agriculture Minister Tummala Nageswara Rao has said.

He asked the agriculture and allied departments to work together to help farmers assess local conditions and prepare for alternative crops, particularly pulses and oilseeds.

The Minister directed officials to draw up and implement irrigation plans under the supervision of district collectors, taking into account water available in reservoirs to protect standing crops.

He also asked scientists to develop groundnut varieties suited to farmers’ requirements and market demand. Responding to requests from farmers in the erstwhile Mahabubnagar district, he said steps would be taken to provide subsidised sprinklers for crops.

analysis.tldr: Telangana's push for water-saving crops could shift rural incomes and local food supplies, affecting prices of everyday kitchen staples like pulses and oilseeds.
the_story: The Telangana government has advised farmers to grow short-duration pulses and oilseeds for the upcoming rabi (yasangi) season instead of water-heavy crops.
Agriculture Minister Tummala Nageswara Rao stated the advice is due to likely water shortages caused by the continued impact of El Niño (a weather pattern that usually brings dry conditions).
The Minister directed agriculture and allied departments to help farmers assess local water availability and prepare alternative crop plans.

District collectors will supervise irrigation plans based on water left in reservoirs, and scientists have been asked to develop suitable groundnut varieties alongside plans for subsidised sprinklers.
analysis.what_happened: The Telangana government warned farmers about expected water shortages driven by El Niño. Because reservoirs may lack enough water for heavy-irrigation crops, officials are officially steering farmers toward pulses (like lentils) and oilseeds (like groundnut) that need less water and time to grow.
analysis.analogy: It is like a household noticing their water tank is only half full for the summer, so the family decides to plant small potted herbs instead of a thirsty garden that needs daily hose-watering.
why_it_matters_india: Telangana farmers switch to pulses and oilseeds -> local water usage drops to conserve reservoir levels.
Shift in crop production -> changes the supply volumes of specific grains and oils coming out of the state.
Local harvest changes -> influences regional market prices for pulses and edible oils.
Broader food supply adjustments -> can feed into national inflation rates (the speed at which everyday living costs rise) if similar shifts happen across regions.

impacts.rationale: Growing more pulses and oilseeds locally helps boost supply, which can keep food prices stable or lower — generally good for household grocery budgets.

impacts.target: Agri-input stocks (like irrigation equipment and seed companies)
impacts.rationale: Government plans to provide subsidised sprinklers and develop new groundnut varieties can boost business for companies selling farming tools.

watch_next: Updates on reservoir water levels in Telangana as the rabi season progresses
Further announcements on subsidies and distribution dates for farming sprinklers
analysis.caveats: This card is based entirely on the provided article text detailing Telangana's agricultural advisory and El Niño concerns.

events.article_text:
Australia Close to Finalizing Gas Reservation Plan for LNG Exporters

What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the…

Crude oil prices were on course to book a weekly gain earlier today amid a flurry of tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz—and outside it, too. Reports citing President Trump as saying productive talks were being held with Iran failed to allay concerns driving the benchmarks higher.

At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $102.83 per barrel, with West Texas Intermediate at $90.33 per barrel, both slightly down from opening but higher compared to their opening prices this week.

Earlier this week, analysts from Kpler said that the number of tankers traversing the Strait of Hormuz has dropped to the lowest in two months amid renewed attacks on vessels in the waterway—right after tanker-tracking outlets said oil flows out of Hormuz are back to pre-war levels.

“Crude crossing the strait fell 27% from a wartime high the week before, to at least 10.1 million barrels a day,” the analysts reported, as the firm counted only seven commodity carriers traversing the strait on Tuesday. This was the lowest figure since late July, the analysts said.

Meanwhile, news emerged of Iran striking a tanker in the Gulf of Oman, which is where Saudi Arabia conducts its ship-to-ship transfers to get its oil out of the Gulf. Between September 28 and October 2, there were at least 12 attacks on tankers carrying crude oil, liquid petroleum gas, and liquefied natural gas, according to data from a U.S. Navy-led joint information center on maritime transport.

Also this week, the U.S. stepped up its sanction pressure on Iran, despite those productive talks. The latest sanctions targeted individuals, tankers, and networks, Reuters reported earlier today. There were 17 newly sanctioned tankers carrying Iranian crude, fuels, and petrochemicals.

On top of all this, there is a growing shortage of tankers, thanks to record-high freight rates offered for routes involving the Persian Gulf, because of the high risk of an attack. Ship-to-ship transfers have also tightened the supply of vessels for other parts of the world, driving physical delivery oil prices higher still.

analysis.tldr: When global crude oil prices stay above $100 because of tanker attacks and blocked shipping routes, everyday items in India get more expensive to make and buy, and running a car becomes costlier.
the_story: Brent crude (the international benchmark for oil prices) was trading at $102.83 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate (another major oil benchmark) was at $90.33 per barrel.

Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dropped to a two-month low, with crude crossing the strait falling 27% from the previous week's wartime high to 10.1 million barrels a day, according to analysts from Kpler.

Between September 28 and October 2, there were at least 12 attacks on tankers carrying crude oil, liquid petroleum gas, and liquefied natural gas, including an Iranian strike on a tanker in the Gulf of Oman.
The U.S. increased sanction pressure on Iran by targeting individuals, tankers, and networks, including 17 newly sanctioned tankers carrying Iranian crude, fuels, and petrochemicals.
A growing shortage of tankers and record-high freight (shipping) rates due to attack risks and ship-to-ship transfers have driven physical delivery oil prices higher.
analysis.what_happened: Global oil prices jumped and stayed above $100 per barrel because ongoing attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman caused tanker traffic to drop to a two-month low. This supply bottleneck was made worse by new U.S. sanctions on Iranian tankers and a shortage of available ships.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major highway carrying food trucks getting blocked by repeated accidents; even if food is sitting in the warehouses, it takes fewer trucks and higher transport costs to get it to your local market, causing prices to spike.
why_it_matters_india: Attacks and sanctions choke oil transport in the Middle East -> fewer tankers reach the market, driving global crude oil prices above $100 per barrel.
India imports a vast majority of its oil -> costlier crude means India must spend significantly more dollars to buy the same amount of oil.
To buy those expensive dollars, demand for the US dollar rises, causing the rupee to weaken (each rupee buys fewer dollars).
Costlier imported oil filters into domestic fuel, transport, and manufacturing costs -> driving up inflation (the rate at which prices rise) for everyday goods in India.

impacts.rationale: Attacks on tankers and shrinking shipping routes restrict the physical supply of oil, pushing prices up — bad for a net oil importer like India.
India needs more US dollars to pay for costlier oil imports, which weakens the rupee — generally bad because it makes all imported goods pricier.
Higher crude prices raise the cost of transportation and manufacturing, leading to costlier everyday items and transport — bad for household budgets.
Raw material costs for fuel rise when crude is above $100, which can translate to higher pump prices — bad for vehicle owners and commuters.

watch_next: Updates on tanker traffic volume through the Strait of Hormuz
Further developments regarding U.S. sanctions on Iranian shipping networks
analysis.caveats: If diplomatic talks between the U.S. and Iran yield sudden breakthroughs or emergency oil releases happen, shipping fears could ease and pull crude prices back down.

analysis.tldr: A weaker rupee makes imported goods like electronics and crude oil more expensive for everyday Indians, pushing up daily living costs.
the_story: On Thursday, the Indian rupee dropped to a two-month low against the US dollar.
The decline happened because FPIs (Foreign Portfolio Investors, big overseas entities investing in local markets) sold off their Indian investments.
This selling was driven by rising US bond yields (the return the US government pays to people who lend it money) and high demand for the US dollar.
Custodian banks (financial institutions that hold securities for safe-keeping) kept buying dollars, showing that money is actively leaving India.
analysis.what_happened: The Indian rupee fell to a two-month low because big overseas investors pulled their money out of India. This happened as US bond yields went up, making safe US investments more attractive, while heavy demand for US dollars from banks created intense pressure on the Indian currency.
analysis.analogy: It is like people at a ticket counter suddenly deciding to trade Indian rupees for US dollars because the line next door is offering a better, safer deal, making rupees pile up and lose their relative value.
why_it_matters_india: US bond yields rise -> global investors pull money out of emerging markets like India to chase better, safer returns in the US.
FPIs sell Indian assets -> foreign investors convert their rupees back into US dollars.
Heavy demand for dollars -> the rupee weakens (each rupee buys fewer dollars).
A weaker rupee -> importing things like crude oil and electronics costs more, which can raise domestic inflation (rising prices of goods over time).

impacts.rationale: Directly reported in the text as facing intense market pressure from foreign outflows and dollar buying, which hurts importers and travelers.
A weaker rupee increases the cost of imported goods like oil, leading to higher everyday expenses—bad for consumers.
It costs more rupees to buy the same amount of foreign goods when the local currency sinks.

watch_next: Whether US bond yields continue to rise or stabilize
Further data on foreign portfolio investor buying and selling patterns in India
analysis.caveats: The article text is relatively short and embedded within promotional text, but it clearly states the core facts regarding the rupee drop and its causes.

events.headline: Mint Quick Edit | India’s latest GST reforms should help turn production more competitive

items.title: Mint Quick Edit | India’s latest GST reforms should help turn production more competitive
items.summary: The broad aim of the GST Council's reform package is to ease processes and compliance. A big gain will be the working capital that would be unlocked—especially for businesses with long or highly taxed supply chains. The changes deserve a warm welcome.

events.article_text:
Data shows that India’s GST rate cuts of September 2025 served as a consumption stimulus. Reforms approved by the GST Council on Thursday covering procedural aspects of GST 2.0 could give production a push.

Apart from making it easier to register for this tax, offering a breather on being arrested for misdeeds and easing penalties, the package promises taxpayers faster approval of claims, among other benefits. The broad aim is to ease procedures and hence compliance.

While the regime has matured and revenues have stabilized, it had gained much complexity along the way. A common taxpayer complaint among businesses has been how long it takes to get refunds, as often due for input tax credit pile-ups. Delays needlessly soak up working capital and make it harder to rotate money competitively across production cycles.

By design, a value-addition tax like GST is supposed to relieve commerce of the burden of tax cascades along value chains. But since money has time value, that gain kicks in fully only if no cash is held up.

Speedy releases will be particularly useful for industries with long or highly taxed input networks. Overdue these reforms may be, but they deserve a hearty welcome.

analysis.tldr: Easier tax rules and faster refunds mean businesses will have more free cash to run smoothly, which could ultimately make Indian-made goods more competitive and help grow the economy.
the_story: The GST Council approved new procedural reforms on Thursday, following previous tax rate cuts in September 2025 that boosted consumption.
The new package makes tax registration easier, relaxes penalty and arrest rules for tax mistakes, and promises faster approval of tax claims and refunds.

Businesses have long complained about slow tax refunds—especially for input tax credit (tax paid on raw materials) pile-ups—which trap working capital (money used for daily business operations) and slow down production.
The reforms aim to remove these bottlenecks so money can move faster across production cycles, fulfilling the original goal of GST to relieve commerce from tax burdens.
analysis.what_happened: The GST Council approved procedural changes known as GST 2.0 to fix the system's growing complexity. Businesses were suffering because delayed refunds tied up their cash, making it hard to rotate money smoothly. The new package fixes this by speeding up claims, easing penalties, and simplifying tax registration.
analysis.analogy: It is like a shopkeeper whose change is stuck in a heavy cash register, stopping them from buying fresh stock; freeing that cash lets them run the shop much faster.
why_it_matters_india: GST Council approves procedural tax reforms ->
Tax refunds and claims are processed much faster for businesses ->
Companies get their trapped working capital back sooner instead of waiting ->
Firms can rotate money faster, lowering production costs and boosting Indian manufacturing competitiveness

impacts.rationale: Faster cash flow and lower compliance friction help factories produce goods more efficiently, which is generally good for industrial growth.

impacts.target: Working capital costs for Indian businesses
impacts.rationale: Easier rules and quicker refunds mean companies do not need to borrow as heavily just to cover stuck tax money—good for business health.

Reactions and feedback from business owners and industry associations on the new procedures
analysis.caveats: Only the headline and opinion text were available, so the actual speed of implementation by tax authorities remains to be seen.

events.headline: US Has Opened Direct Talks With Myanmar Government, Report Claims

items.title: US Has Opened Direct Talks With Myanmar Government, Report Claims
items.summary: The outreach, which marks a significant shift in U.S. policy, is aimed at curbing online scamming operations and gaining access to the country's rare earth deposits.

events.article_text:
Yesterday, Reuters published a report stating that the Trump administration has begun direct talks with Myanmar’s military-installed government for the first time since the 2021 coup, marking a significant change in U.S. policy toward the country.

According to the report, which was authored by Reuters’ Simon Lewis and cited seven current and former U.S. officials and others familiar with the ‌policy shift, this engagement has so far focused on discreet issues, such as efforts to shut down the online scam centers, but “could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits.”

The report claimed that U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance “joined talks” with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw on September 15-16. The meeting was nominally aimed at securing the release of detained American businessman Adam Castillo, but also provided an opening for further engagement, four of the sources told Reuters.

Whether or not it is sustained, the engagement marks an important shift in U.S. policy towards Myanmar. When Min Aung Hlaing seized power in a coup in 2021, terminating a decade of political and economic reforms, the U.S. government quickly reimposed economic sanctions on senior generals and businesses linked to the military. The following year, it downgraded its diplomatic representation in the country, reverting to the policy that pertained between 1987 and 2012, when the U.S. was represented by a chief of mission rather than a fully credentialed ambassador.

The Reuters report also identified how Myanmar’s new military government used the detention of Castillo, a former head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar who was arrested at Yangon airport in June on opaque charges, in order to advance diplomatic re-engagement with Washington.

The September meeting between Vance and Min Aung Hlaing was preceded by back-channel negotiations between U.S. and Myanmar officials aimed at securing Castillo’s release. During these talks, Reuters reported, Myanmar “only asked for an official engagement at the right level with the U.S. government” in return.

The report makes clear that these were not the first engagements between U.S. and Myanmar officials. In June, the two sides held meetings in Tokyo; one source cited by the news agency said that in addition to Vance, “officials from the Treasury Department, which oversees sanctions, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Pentagon took part.” Josh Kurlantzick of the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) wrote yesterday that several sources had also told him that prior to Vance’s visit to Naypyidaw, “U.S. officials had been secretly meeting with officials from Myanmar in Japan.”

The purpose of this engagement, the Reuters report states, was to combat the online scamming operations that have become deeply rooted in Myanmar since the coup, and which have defrauded Americans of billions of dollars. It added that “U.S. officials also discussed access to Myanmar’s massive ​deposits of heavy rare earths,” most of which are located in areas of northern Myanmar currently under the control of rebel forces including the Kachin Independence Army (KIA).

Myanmar’s rare earth deposits have gradually become something of an idée fixe for certain elements of the Trump administration, as it seeks to reduce its heavy reliance on China, which controls a large part of the world’s supply of these critical minerals.

In July 2025, Reuters reported that administration officials had “heard competing proposals” for changes to U.S. policy aimed at gaining access to the rare earth deposits in Kachin State. “Among the proposals,” it reported, “are one advocating talks with Myanmar’s ruling junta to get a peace deal with the Kachin Independence Army rebels and another calling for the U.S. to instead work directly with the KIA without engaging the junta.”

Among those advancing these proposals was none other than Adam Castillo, who was present during a July 17 meeting at Vice President J.D. Vance’s office in Washington.

It is hard to know how far things will proceed from here. The Reuters report makes clear that Vance “has also met in person and virtually with the democratic opposition and ethnic armed groups fighting the military,” and the State Department told the news agency that its engagement with the Min Aung Hlaing administration “does not diminish its relationships with other groups.”

Any step toward further re-engagement with Naypyidaw, let alone a dropping of U.S. sanctions against Min Aung Hlaing and other senior officials, is likely to prompt strong criticism. While the new quasi-civilian government has attempted to project an image of control and normalcy, the political situation in the country remains febrile. The post-coup civil war, which continues despite the inauguration of the new government, has now killed more than 100,000 people and displaced 3.8 million more. In a report released yesterday, the U.N. Development Programme stated that more than two in three people in Myanmar are now in “multidimensional poverty” or are at risk of falling into it, due to the “simultaneous collapse” of the healthcare and education systems, and the atrophying of the economy.

Since taking office as president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has embarked on a diplomatic charm offensive aimed at consolidating key partnerships and normalizing Naypyidaw’s relationship with key partners, including the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Indeed, the former general has just departed from Malaysia, where, in another notable policy reversal, he was accorded full state honors by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. He has also visited Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, and Thailand in recent months, in pursuit of Myanmar’s full reintegration into the 11-nation bloc.

Re-engagement with the U.S., even to a limited degree, would be another diplomatic victory for Min Aung Hlaing. Whether this would end

analysis.tldr: Direct talks between the US and Myanmar's military government could gradually alter rare-earth mineral supply chains in Asia, though the direct ripple effects on everyday Indian household finances remain minimal.
the_story: Reuters reported that the Trump administration has started direct talks with Myanmar's military-installed government for the first time since the 2021 coup.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Michael Vance met with Myanmar president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw on September 15-16, ostensibly to secure the release of detained American businessman Adam Castillo.
Discussions have focused on shutting down online scam centers and could expand to Myanmar's rare-earth mineral deposits, which the US wants to access to reduce reliance on China.
Prior meetings occurred in Tokyo in June involving US officials from the Treasury, Homeland Security, and the Pentagon, following back-channel negotiations.
Min Aung Hlaing has also embarked on a broader diplomatic charm offensive, recently receiving full state honors in Malaysia and visiting other ASEAN nations.
analysis.what_happened: The US government has opened direct diplomatic talks with Myanmar's military rulers, reversing a policy of isolation that began after the 2021 coup. This shift is driven by US goals to shut down online scam operations and secure access to Myanmar's rare-earth minerals to decrease reliance on China.
analysis.analogy: It is like a strict shopkeeper finally sitting down to talk with a troublesome supplier because they desperately need a rare ingredient that only that supplier has.
why_it_matters_india: US shifts policy toward Myanmar -> US seeks alternatives to Chinese rare-earth minerals -> Potential reordering of critical mineral supply chains in Asia -> Broad geopolitical ripple effects for regional manufacturing competitors like India.
Diplomatic normalization by Western powers -> Myanmar secures legitimacy and reintegration into regional blocs (ASEAN) -> Shifts geopolitical alignment in India's immediate eastern neighborhood.

impacts.rationale: If the US successfully secures access to Myanmar's rare-earth deposits, it could reduce global dependency on Chinese supply monopolies, affecting high-tech manufacturing costs worldwide.
This specific diplomatic engagement has a very indirect connection to Indian equities, leaving domestic market trends driven primarily by local economic factors.

watch_next: Whether the US formally eases economic sanctions on Myanmar's senior generals and military-linked businesses
Further developments regarding US access to Myanmar's rare-earth mineral deposits in Kachin State
Reactions from regional groups like ASEAN and neighboring China to closer US-Myanmar engagement
analysis.caveats: The article cuts off before detailing the full conclusion of Myanmar's diplomatic push, and it remains uncertain how far the US will actually proceed with policy reversals.

events.headline: Not just AI. China is building technologies that challenge U.S. dominance

items.title: Not just AI. China is building technologies that challenge U.S. dominance
items.summary: From batteries and solar panels to drones and satellites, China is building tech capabilities that extend well beyond AI, writes Steve Feldstein in his new book, "Bytes and Bullets: Global Rivalries, Big Tech, and the New Shape of Modern Warfare."

events.article_text:
While China is engaged in a fierce struggle with the U.S. for AI supremacy, it is accelerating its development of other future technologies. In 2024, Chinese investors put nearly $1 trillion in clean-­energy capex for renewables, electricity grids, and energy storage. As a result, China now makes 70% of the world’s EVs, its companies are responsible for 80%–­85% of global solar photovoltaic manufacturing, and they oversee more than 75% of global battery production. Writes Columbia University scholar Tim Wu, “If we set AI aside for a moment and assume that these technologies represent the future, it is clear who is ahead.”

Other benchmarks reach a similar conclusion. Take, for example, the Australian Strategic Policy Institute’s “Critical Technology Tracker,” which analyzes China and the United States’ research capacity across ­74 current and emerging technologies. The latest data from December 2025 indicated that China led research in nearly 90% of crucial technologies, including nuclear energy, synthetic biology, and small satellites. The results revealed a “drastic reversal,” writes Xiaoying You in Nature. At the beginning of the century, American scientists held an enduring advantage in more than 90% of assessed technologies, with China leading in less than 5% of them; but in the intervening 25 years, Chinese researchers flipped the balance.

While the findings are striking, some caveats are in order. Most importantly, the authors measured cited pieces of research as opposed to deployable or applied technology. It is one thing to publish theoretical concepts. It is quite another to come up with a manufacturing process and actually produce specific items. When it comes to innovations like jet engines (a task that remains stubbornly elusive for Chinese engineers), whether research translates to manufacturing is a key question. As the authors acknowledge, “If you’re good at origami but don’t yet excel at making decent paper, are you really good at origami?” Nonetheless, the conclusions are sobering and signify how swiftly China has narrowed the scientific gap with the U.S.

China’s success in the consumer drone industry underscores its growing technological power. Da Jiang Innovations (DJI), which is based in Shenzhen, holds more than 70% of the global consumer drone market. In 2022, the size of that market was about $30.6 billion; it is expected to grow to $55.8 billion by 2030. While studying at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, founder and CEO Frank Wang started DJI in 2006. Rather than work out of a dorm room, Wang and two of his classmates rented a small office across the border in Shenzhen. He started selling drone control systems for hobbyists making their own DIY units. By 2013, DJI released its first preassembled “ready-­to-­fly” drone, the Phantom 1, which sold for less than $700. The product was a hit —­ the cost was reasonable, and the unit came with “serious hardware,” making it stand out from the cheap toy versions being sold at similar price points.

Today, DJI is a behemoth: it has over 14,000 employees and no close competitors. Its drones are ubiquitous, including in the U.S. They are used by first responders to respond to emergencies and by hobbyists to take panoramic photos. They have also become an important fixture on the battlefield, particularly in Ukraine. Both sides rely heavily on DJI drones to surveil troop movements, guide artillery, and identify enemy emplacements. China has reportedly shipped millions of dollars’ worth of DJI units to Russia during the conflict.

But it is not just Wang’s resourcefulness and tenacity that is responsible for DJI’s market dominance. U.S. tech executives confided to me that there was no way a U.S. company could replicate DJI’s success. The industry’s understanding was that DJI scaled due to massive subsidies from the Chinese government, affording it major cost advantages. Reporting from The Washington Post confirmed these claims, despite DJI’s assertions that it had not accepted any funding from the Chinese government. Reporters reviewed company documents and other sensitive information showing that four investment entities “owned or administered by Beijing” invested in DJI, including a government asset manager who played a key role in “promoting partnerships between private enterprises and the Chinese military.”

Not only did state subsidies play an important role in propping up the company, but DJI also benefited from being part of China’s competitive drone ecosystem, which spawned an array of service providers producing advanced components at cut-­rate prices. Few other countries could compete. When a Taiwanese drone manufacturer tried to replace its Chinese-­made engines, it searched far and wide for alternatives, even going to Australia, where it found that an equivalent engine “would cost 20 times more.” The company eventually inked a deal with a local supplier, but only after convincing the bidder to lower its prices “as an act of virtue” to support Taiwan’s defense.

Like other Chinese firms and products (such as TikTok), geopolitics have caught up to DJI. In December 2025, the Federal Communications Commission blacklisted all new foreign-­made drones and components from the U.S. market over concerns that they posed “an unacceptable risk” to national security. While the directive didn’t directly name DJI, given the company’s 80% share of America’s consumer drone market, the implication was clear: DJI drones were no longer welcome in the U.S. (For now, the FCC’s rule doesn’t impact DJI’s unmanned aircraft already in use; it only applies to new drone sales.) In short, today’s geopolitics has made DJI’s position increasingly untenable for America’s interests.

Experts remain divided about how the U.S. and China stack up on science and technology. In certain sectors, American research continues to lead; in other areas, China appears to be supplanting the U.S. What is clear is that the days of China as an “imi

analysis.tldr: China's massive rise in clean-energy and technology manufacturing means Indian companies face fierce low-cost competition globally, but also cheaper imported green technology components.
the_story: In 2024, Chinese investors spent nearly $1 trillion on clean-energy capex, leading China to make 70% of the world’s electric vehicles (EVs), 80% to 85% of solar photovoltaic manufacturing, and over 75% of battery production.

Data from December 2025 by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute shows China now leads research in nearly 90% of 74 crucial technologies (such as nuclear energy and small satellites), a complete reversal from 25 years ago.
Chinese drone maker DJI holds over 70% of the global consumer drone market, scaled up through government subsidies, a strong local parts ecosystem, and low prices.
In December 2025, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission blacklisted new foreign-made drones and components due to national security risks, targeting market leaders like DJI.
analysis.what_happened: China has rapidly overtaken the U.S. in research and manufacturing across key future technologies like clean energy, batteries, and drones. This dominance was built through massive government funding, heavy investments totaling nearly $1 trillion in 2024, and deeply integrated domestic supply chains that make it nearly impossible for Western competitors to match their prices.
analysis.analogy: It is like a mega-factory that can pump out goods so cheaply because the local government pays half the electric bill, making it impossible for a corner shop down the street to sell the same item without losing money.
why_it_matters_india: Chinese firms produce extremely cheap solar panels, batteries, and green energy equipment.
Indian renewable energy companies import these cut-rate Chinese parts to build solar and EV projects at a lower cost.
However, Indian manufacturing firms face a tough battle trying to compete against heavily subsidized Chinese goods flooding global markets.
India must balance buying cheap green technology to meet its climate goals while protecting its own domestic factories through import duties.

impacts.rationale: Cheaper imported Chinese solar panels and clean energy gear help lower overall infrastructure and power costs in India, which is generally good for consumers.

impacts.target: Indian renewable energy stocks (like Tata Power, Adani Green)
impacts.rationale: Access to ultra-cheap global solar and battery parts helps these companies build power plants more profitably, which is positive for investors.

impacts.target: Indian domestic manufacturing stocks (clean tech and electronics)
impacts.rationale: Local Indian factories struggle to compete against subsidized, cut-rate Chinese hardware, which poses challenges for local manufacturing growth.

watch_next: Whether the Indian government increases import taxes or trade barriers on Chinese solar panels and green technology
How fast Indian domestic companies can scale up their own manufacturing capacity for electric vehicles and batteries
analysis.caveats: The research metrics cited measure academic papers and potential rather than finished manufacturing output in every single sector, meaning actual commercial dominance can vary.

events.headline: DDG Nordquist: Trade continues apace, showing resiliency

items.title: DDG Nordquist: Trade continues apace, showing resiliency
items.summary: Speaking at a panel on leadership in global trade at the 17th Swiss Coffee Trade Association (SCTA) Forum on 1 October in Montreux, Deputy Director-General DJ Nordquist said that the WTO and its basic functions are increasingly important as geopolitics and economic security now play a much bigger role in trade decisions, with companies having to think more about geopolitical exposure, security of supply, regulatory risk and resilience.

events.article_text:
Supply chains have rerouted and adapted, with trade growth continuing to defy expectations, she told forum participants.

"At the start of 2025, WTO economists projected that trade growth would be negative and instead, it grew 4.6 per cent for the year, significantly outpacing global GDP growth, with 72 per cent of worldwide trade still occurring under most-favoured nation rules. Partners may be changing within the top trading economies, but trade has still been occurring and adjusting to a 'new normal.'"

WTO members have to recognize the reality that trade policy "no longer sits in a separate box" and that governments are pursuing different industrial strategies, climate objectives, resilience and economic-security objectives, DDG Nordquist argued.

"One man's protectionism may be another's economic security," she noted. The question for the trading system is how do these different governance and economic models coexist without creating unnecessary barriers, discrimination, or damaging economies.

This is where the WTO can make a difference, by improving transparency through improved notifications, promoting dialogue and reforming its rulebook, which is more than three decades old.

"We need to be realistic," DDG Nordquist said. "In the current environment characterized by geopolitical tensions and lack of trust, a grand multilateral bargain is hardly possible."

"But that does not make the WTO less relevant. In some ways, it makes the basic functions of the WTO more important," through its common foundation of rules, inclusiveness and its infrastructure for transparency, monitoring and dialogue.

A successful WTO "does not require solving every disagreement among 166 members," but rather showing that members with very different interests and economic models can still cooperate and produce better outcomes than fragmentation, she concluded.

Problems viewing this page? If so, please contact [email protected] giving details of the operating system and web browser you are using.

analysis.tldr: Global trade is growing faster than expected despite global tensions, which helps keep foreign markets open for Indian exports.
the_story: At the start of 2025, WTO (World Trade Organization, a global group that sets rules for trade between countries) economists projected negative trade growth, but trade actually grew by 4.6 per cent for the year.

Global trade significantly outpaced global GDP (Gross Domestic Product, the total value of goods and services produced in a country), with 72 per cent of worldwide trade happening under standard rules.
DDG (Deputy Director-General) Nordquist stated that trade supply chains have successfully rerouted and adapted to a 'new normal'.
Nordquist noted that trade policy now overlaps with industrial strategies, climate goals, and economic security, where 'one man's protectionism may be another's economic security'.
analysis.what_happened: Global trade grew by 4.6 per cent in 2025 instead of shrinking as economists feared, because supply chains successfully rerouted and adapted to geopolitical tensions. WTO officials report that countries are adjusting their trading partners and strategies to meet new economic security and climate goals.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local delivery network where, if one main bridge closes, delivery drivers simply find alternative routes so packages still keep arriving on time.
why_it_matters_india: Global trade continues to grow robustly at 4.6 per cent instead of slowing down.
Demand for manufactured goods and services remains active worldwide as supply chains adapt.
Indian exporters find steady international markets for their products despite global political tensions.
A stable global trade environment supports overall economic growth and export revenues in India.

impacts.rationale: Stronger global trade demand supports corporate earnings for Indian companies that sell abroad, which is generally good for stock market investors.
Resilient global economic activity encourages foreign clients to keep spending on technology services, benefiting Indian IT firms.
Steady export earnings bring in foreign currency, helping stabilize the rupee value, which lowers the cost of imported goods like oil.

watch_next: Future WTO updates on trade policy changes and new rules
Export growth data from India's Ministry of Commerce
analysis.caveats: Geopolitical tensions and protectionist policies could still create sudden barriers that disrupt specific supply chains.

history.title: A speech that cost India 20% of its currency
history.where: United States, felt hardest in India
history.what: Fed chairman Ben Bernanke suggested in testimony that the Fed might slow its bond buying "in the next few meetings". He did not change any policy. Within four months the rupee had fallen from 55 to 68 per dollar and India was labelled one of the "Fragile Five".
history.why: Years of near-zero US rates had pushed investors into emerging markets hunting for yield. India ran a large current account deficit — importing far more than it exported, with gold and oil the biggest items — and was therefore dependent on that foreign money continuing to arrive. The hint that the tide might turn was enough; no actual policy change was needed.
history.impact: The rupee fell about 20% in four months. Indian bond yields spiked, the stock market fell sharply, and the RBI raised rates into an already slowing economy to defend the currency.
history.policy: The RBI opened a special concessional window to attract dollar deposits from Indians abroad, raising about $34 billion. Gold import duties were raised steeply to curb the import bill. And in 2016 India adopted a formal inflation-targeting framework, which addressed the underlying cause.
history.consequence: India's current account deficit narrowed sharply and reserves were rebuilt to levels that made the 2018 and 2022 dollar shocks far less painful. The gold import duty also created a large smuggling industry — an unintended consequence that took years to unwind.
history.pattern: An economy dependent on foreign capital is hostage to a foreign central bank's tone, not just its decisions. The vulnerability is built during the good years, when the money is arriving and nobody asks why.
history.india_echo: This is the single clearest lesson for an Indian investor about why the Fed matters here. Nothing changed in India that summer. The Nifty fell anyway, because the marginal buyer of Indian shares sits in New York.
history.watch_for: India's current account deficit as a share of GDP, and the share of the market owned by foreign investors. Together they size the exposure.
